To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the LPG of Leishmania mexicam is not required for midgut attachment to Lutzomyia (Lutzomyia) longipalpis.

(1) LPG is essential for L. mexicana and Leishmania guyanensis attachment to L. mexicana, (2) Leishmania braziliensis attachment is LPG-dependent, but the role of LPG in attachment is not as strong as in other species, (3) gp63 is essential for LPG-independent L. mexicana attachment to the midgut epithelial cells of L. mexicana.
LPG is essential for Leishmania major attachment to the midgut in the vector Phlebotomon papatasi, whereas LPG-independent binding occurs in the vector Ph. perniciosus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of surface molecules in parasite attachment to the vector midgut, which is the first crucial step in Leishmania infection of the vector.
the identification of parasite molecules involved in the attachment of Leishmanias to their sand fly vectors.
the identification of Leishmania attachment factors to the sand fly gut, and provides a new tool for further investigations on Leishmania-sand fly interactions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the LPG-independent parasite binding mechanism in P. perniciosus is not a general feature of Leishmania promastigotes, and that the LPG-mediated parasite binding mechanism in Phlebotomines may be restricted to P. papatasi.
the role of surface glycoproteins in midgut binding is dependent on parasite species and vector species, and is also dependent on the technique used to assess binding.
Leishmania attachment to the sandfly midgut is not a simple process and depends on the parasite species, the vector species and on parasite surface molecules.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
L. major and L. mexicana attachment to the permissive vector P. papatasi is LPG-dependent and that L. major attachment to P. perniciosus and L. amazonensis to L. longpalpis is LPG-independent.
the GPI-anchored L. mexicana proteins LPG and gp63, and the LPG of L. major, play important roles in parasite midgut attachment in L. longipalis and P. papatasi, respectively.
the GPI-anchored L. major L. amazonensis and L. mexicana LPG, as well as the GPI-anchoring of gp63 are essential for midgut binding in the respective vectors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the role of surface glycoproteins and LPG in midgut attachment may be species-specific.

the use of different experimental techniques, in vitro and in vivo, can provide valuable information on the mechanisms of parasite attachment to the midgut, which is essential for the establishment of the Leishmaniasis disease cycle in the vector.
in vitro and in vivo assays provide complementary information, and that the in vivo approach may be more sensitive in identifying parasite surface molecules involved in midgut binding.
